newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU adopting restraint on wheat refunds - official.
newsitem.headline: EU adopting restraint on wheat refunds - official.

text.p: The European Commission is reluctant to award high wheat export refunds for as long as a wide gap remains between lowest and highest bids at its weekly grain tender, a farm official at the European Commission said.
"The Commission is in a difficult situation. What do you want it to do? We have entered a turbulent period in which we have seen some very low bids," the official said.
"Once you have given four, five, six, seven, eight Ecus (per tonne in subsidy), you can't give 15 Ecus a week later."
The official was speaking in a general sense before bids were announced for the latest weekly subsidy auction to be held in Brussels later on Thursday.
In France, bids ranged between 5.31 and 11.95 Ecus per tonne for a total volume of 325,500 tonnes of soft or common wheat.
Last week, the Commission awarded 91,200 tonnes of wheat from the open market with a maximum refund of 7.49 Ecus.
Exporters had bid for 371,000 tonnes at subsidies between 4.50 and 14.99 Ecus.

The official said Brussels would study "very closely" the structure of bids -- the relationship between volumes and refunds and the way in which bids are spread out -- but could not in any case promise any "miracles".

"It is a technical issue. Nobody can change the situation," the official said, referring to a continuing discrepancy in the export market between traders long of licences and those short of refunds they need to execute grain deals.
The rift opened up after world wheat prices gained about $25 per tonne from the lowest levels around $140 per tonne earlier this year.
The EU is under pressure to increase subsidies to help some shippers cover loss-making positions while other exporters are chasing subsidy levels lower, analysts have said.
But the official indicated Brussels would not bail out the remaining market shorts.
"As long as there are low (bids for) refunds, we will align ourselves to those," the official said. "We will examine the levels of bids and take the best ones."
"We cannot 'make a gesture'. We have to respect budgetary constraints," the official said, adding that the Commission's task was to export the maximum amount at the lowest penalty.
The official said it was difficult to assess the exact situation exporters were facing, as well as the real need for licences between now and the end of the July/June season.
"Every time we give refunds, people come back with new requirements. We don't understand any more."
In this official's view, new requests for licences were linked to old contracts originally slated for other exporting countries and which were being gradually switched to Europe.

The official also stressed the Commission's primary policy objective was to ensure smooth supplies at affordable prices to the domestic market and that exports were secondary to this. The European Commission would be prepared to consider halting the current export campaign earlier than expected if internal prices continued a recent strong rally.
Traders say domestic prices have been fired up by export demand for the old crop and early fears of drought affecting yields on the new crop.
-- Paule Bonjean, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
